comments.text: This is indeed a very interesting question! I’ve also asked myself that time and time again, along the path of slowly discovering what this FP thing is all about over the course of my career. It does look wonderful, it does save you a lot of effort in some cases, where “some” is a vast swathes of computational problems. And its so damn elegant. A lot of examples are thrown around were a bunch of lambda calculus can result in 10-20 fold reduction in source code size. So where’s the catch?There has to be something wrong right? Well recently I stumbled upon a clojure conf talk that tried to tackle precisely this question. [VIDEO] The short of it is that its more of a historical inertia and chance than any specific hidden gotcha. Fascinating talk.

comments.why_zh: 关于编程语言整体的有趣讨论。

comments.text_zh: 我知道答案，多亏看了 Richard Feldman 最近一个关于函数式编程为什么还没流行起来的视频。我推荐看看，里面有一些关于编程语言整体的有趣讨论，在 YouTube 上：[VIDEO] 总之，private 给你的正是每个人都想从编程语言里得到的东西：模块化。我们希望能够向某些代码暴露一个 API，同时让它有一些我们看不见的内部运作，因为：1. 如果我们知道它们不能被触碰，我们对程序就有一些隐式保证。比如，即使我们试图发起调用来让鼠标指针移出屏幕，它也不能移出屏幕。2. 对程序员来说，理解 API 更简单，而 API 可能只有包含所有 private 的模块本身大小的 1%。3. 我可以修改我的 private 而不破坏你的调用。本质上，用 Semvar 的话说，这是次版本号变更，而不是破坏性的大版本变更。4. 让不可能的状态成为不可能！通过守护状态。所有这些都需要模块化，而 OO 用类和私有成员来提供这种模块化。Elm 用模块和 exposing 关键字（或者没有它！）作为对比。JS 模块类似，没有 export 就能让你隐藏某些东西。你确实导出的那个东西可以用于状态或功能。还有一个老的 IIFE 技巧也是这么工作的。把所有东西都公开是个坏主意，因为你会错过模块化的好处。不确定 Ruby 怎么隐藏东西，我有一阵没用它了，但我确定有一个
comments.text: I know the answer, thanks to watching a recent video by Richard Feldman on why functional programming isn’t popular yet. I recommend watching it for some interesting talk about programming languages in general, it’s on YouTube at [VIDEO] Anyway what privates give you is what everyone wants from a programming language: modularity. We want to be able to expose an api to some code and for it to have some inner workings that we don’t see because: 1. If we know they can’t be touched we have some implicit guarantees about our program. E.g. the mouse pointer cannot go off screen even if we try to make a call to do that. 2. It is simpler for a programmer to understand the api which might be 1% of the size of the module itself with all private’s. 3. I can change my private’s without breaking your calls. Essentially a minor version change in Semvar parlance instead of a major breaking change. 4. Make impossible state impossible! By guarding the state. All these things require modularity, and OO uses classes and private members to provide that modularity. Elm uses modules and the exposing keyword (or lack of!) as a contrast. JS modules are similar with a lack of an export allowing you to hide something. That something you did export can use for state or functionality. There is an old IIFE trick that works this way also. comments.why_zh: 认为 OOP 因 C++ 而偶然流行。
comments.quote_zh: Richard Feldman 提出了一个（在我看来很有根据的）论点：OO 之所以流行是偶然的，因为 C++。
comments.text_zh: 在思想的市场里，好想法通常没有什么理由会不流行。那才是默认结果。有些好想法最终进入主流/常识，是因为有某种第二因素把它们带到聚光灯下。对语言来说，可能是杀手级应用、大公司投资等等。在 [VIDEO] 中，Richard Feldman 提出了一个（在我看来很有根据的）论点：OO 之所以流行是偶然的，因为 C++。C++ 并没有把 OO 做好，OO 也不是 C++ 的主要好处，它只是恰好随 C++ 一起来的东西。
comments.text: In the market of ideas, there usually isn't any reason that makes the good ideas unpopular. That's the default outcome. Some good ideas eventually make it to mainstream / conventional wisdom because there's some second factor that brings them to the spotlight. For languages it might be a killer app, big corporate investment, etc. In [VIDEO] Richard Feldman puts up a (well founded IMO) argument that OO became accidentally popular because of C++. C++ didn't do OO well, nor was OO the main benefit of C++, it just happened to be something that came with C++.

comments.text_zh: Richard Feldman 在 2019 年就此做了一个有趣的演讲 [0]。他试图回答为什么函数式编程没有成为主流，但这里我们提出的问题正好相反，而我认为原因有很多是相同的。网络效应：这些语言中有很多早年就是主流，并获得了很多人的支持，而这些人也投入于它们持续被采用和成功。平台独占性：一些公司在自己的平台上推广自己的语言生态，而那些语言往往是 OOP/多范式语言。具体到 OOP，我们得问：为什么 C++/Java 这种特定风格的 OOP 成了常态？为什么 Eiffel、Smalltalk 或 Self 没有达到同样的市场？[0] [VIDEO] 编辑：忘了放链接——哎呀。
comments.text: Richard Feldman gave an interesting talk on this in 2019 [0]. He was trying to answer why functional programming isn't mainstream but the opposite is what we're posing here and I think it's for many of the same reasons. Network effects : a lot of these languages were mainstream earlier on and got buy in from a lot of folks who are invested in their continued adoption and success. Platform exclusivity : some companies push their own language ecosystems on their platforms and those languages are often OOP/multi-paradigm languages. Specifically to OOP we have to ask why is the particular style of C++/Java OOP the norm? Why didn't Eiffel, Smalltalk, or Self reach the same market? [0] [VIDEO] edit : forgot the link -- oops.

comments.quote_zh: 如果你想听长篇回答，这是一场来自 Clojure 会议、正好讲这个主题的精彩演讲。
comments.text_zh: 如果你想听长篇回答，这是一场来自 Clojure 会议、正好讲这个主题的精彩演讲。它聚焦于 Clojure 的“函数式”特性，但在我看来，其中所有内容都适用于整个语言（可能也适用于任何优秀的 Lisp）。[VIDEO] 我简短的文字回答（聚焦于 Clojure）：-Python 比 Clojure 早出现了大约 20 年 -Clojure 相对于 Python 等的优势，可能远不如 Python 相对于 C 这种非内存托管、编译型、静态语言的优势那么大。那一整代“脚本”语言都顺风而行，而 Clojure 及其同时代语言则从未真正有过这种势头（尽管 Clojure 等语言在并发和并行方面往往要好得多，这会大有帮助）-陌生的语法（不像 Algol 系）和范式（不是 OOP）——而事实是，当一样东西太异类时，许多程序员会慢慢退避 -没有找到像数据科学、科学计算或 CRUD 网站构建那么大的细分领域 -我认为 Python 聚集了一些很棒的学术细分领域，其中至少有一个（ML/数据科学）人气爆炸式增长。Ruby 拥有 Rails 社区。Clojure 似乎在金融科技领域有一定人气，但还没有一个它主导的大型单一细分领域。
comments.text: This is a great talk on exactly this topic from a Clojure conference, if you want a long answer. It focuses on the “functional” feature of Clojure but all of it applies to the whole language (and probably any good lisp) IMO. [VIDEO] My brief text answer (focused on Clojure): -python has been around about 20 more years than Clojure -the advantages of Clojure vs python/etc probably aren’t nearly as big as python vs a non memory managed, compiled, static language like C. That whole generation of “scripting” languages had the wind at their backs in a way Clojure and its contemporaries never quite will (though Clojure et al tend to be much better at concurrency and parallelism and this will help a lot) -unfamiliar syntax (not Algol like) and paradigm (not oop)- and the truth is many programmers back away slowly when a thing is too alien -hasn’t found a niche as big as data science or scientific computing or CRUD website building - I think python has aggregated some great academic niches, at least one of which (ML/data science) exploded in popularity. Ruby had the rails community. Clojure seems to have some popularity in fintech but has no big single niche yet that it dominates.

comments.why_zh: 关于函数式编程为何不是常态的合理解释。
comments.quote_zh: Richard Feldman [0] 提出了一些最合理的理论，解释函数式编程为什么不是常态。
comments.text_zh: 为什么它没有更流行？我认为 Richard Feldman [0] 提出了一些最合理的理论，解释函数式编程为什么不是常态。你的语言需要成为某个被广泛使用的平台的平台独占语言，或者为某个极受追捧的应用领域提供一个杀手级应用，或者背后有一大笔营销资金来左右观点。自 Feldman 的演讲以来，Python 在人气上的增长快得多——从市场广泛使用这个意义上说……但这主要是因为它成了 PyTorch 以及 AI 相关库/工具/框架的首选脚本语言，而这……就是一个杀手级应用。我喜欢 OCaml。我通过在线学习 INRIA 的课程，开始用它来评估函数式编程。过去四年半我一直在用 Haskell 工作。我用 Zig 做过一些副业项目。多年来我一直是 CL 的铁杆粉丝。我经常问这个问题。我们常说“用最适合这项工作的工具”。这往往意味着“用可用的那个工具”。我认为像 OCaml、Rust、Haskell 等语言可以是“流行”的，但那是就人们喜欢谈论它们、想学它们并且能够使用它们而言（至少，随着潮流来来去去）。这和“被广泛采用”意义上的“流行”不同。[0] [VIDEO]
comments.text: Why isn't it more popular? I think Richard Feldman [0] proposed some of the most reasonable theories as to why functional programming isn't the norm. Your language needs to be the platform-exclusive language for a widely used platform, have a killer application for a highly desired application domain, or be backed by a monster war-chest of marketing money to sway opinions. Since Feldman's talk, Python has grown much faster in popularity in the sense of wide use in the market place... but mostly because it's the scripting language of choice for PyTorch and AI-adjacent libraries/tooling/frameworks which is... a killer application. I like OCaml. I started evaluating functional programming in it by taking the INRIA course online. I spent the last four and half years working in Haskell. I've built some side projects in Zig. I was a CL stan for many years. I asked this question a lot. We often say, "use the best tool for the job." Often that means, "use the tool that's available." I think languages like OCaml, Rust, Haskell etc can be "popular," but in the sense that people like to talk about them and want to learn them and be able to use them (at least, as trends come and go). In terms of newer languages, the only ones I can think of offhand that seem to have serious traction are Swift and to a lesser extent Go. comments.why_zh: 关于 FP 特性被非 FP 语言借鉴的脚注。
comments.text_zh: FP 是一种思维方式，FP 语言为它提供了好用的特性/语法。你也可以用 FP 语言做非 FP 风格的编程。事实上，许多 FP 语言特性已经被非 FP 语言借鉴，以至于人们不再把它们当作“FP”[0]。（比如 JS 的 `.map()` 和 `.reduce()`。现在连 Excel 宏都支持一等函数[1]。）三个能让在 JS 中运用 FP 思维更容易的特性：1. 不可变元组和记录[2] 2. 管道操作符[3] 3. 模式匹配[4] 重大顿悟：根据《Grokking Simplicity》[5]，好的函数式编程不在于避免非纯函数，而在于对它们格外小心。非纯函数依赖被调用的时间，所以最难写对。归根结底，所有软件的目的都是造成某种变更/效果（翻转屏幕像素、把比特保存到存储、发送电子邮件等）。“Functional Core, Imperative Shell”[6] 可能是最有用的 FP 概念。它的做法是把变更/错误/非纯函数推到代码的外围边缘，这样内部代码就能专注于“happy path”。复杂的业务逻辑住在内层核心；外壳通常简单/无分支，所以甚至不需要单元测试。[0]: [VIDEO] [1]: [LINK] [2]: [LINK] [3]: [LINK] [4]: [LINK] [5]: [LINK] [6]: [LINK]
comments.text: FP is a way of thinking, which FP languages give nice features/syntax for. You can do non-FP style programming with an FP language. In fact, many FP language features have been borrowed by non-FP languages to the point people don't consider them "FP" anymore[0]. (Like JS `.map()` and `.reduce()`. Even Excel macros now support first-class functions[1].) Three features that would make FP thinking in JS easier: 1. immutable tuples and records[2] 2. pipe operator[3] 3. pattern matching[4] Major epiphany: According to Grokking Simplicity[5], good functional programming isn't about avoiding impure functions; instead it's about giving extra care to them. Impure functions depend on the time they are called, so they are the most difficult to get right. In the end, the purpose of all software is to cause some type of mutation/effect (flip pixels on a screen, save bits to storage, send email, etc). "Functional Core, Imperative Shell"[6] is probably the most useful FP concept. It is about pushing mutation/errors/impure functions to the outer edges of your code, so the inner code can focus on the "happy path." Complex business logic lives in the inner core; the outer shell is often simple/branchless so unit tests aren't even needed. comments.text: Also related: [VIDEO] Network effects likely explain a big part of it. Many of the "popular" languages today aren't necessarily great languages and adopted for their technical merits. Often they were the only language available on an exclusive platform everyone wanted to develop software on. Other times it was because folks wanted to write a particular kind of application and there just happened to be this framework in this weird language that made the task easy. We probably have more programming languages now than ever before but I think the market for new languages in the mainstream is relatively static. It shifts... but very slowly.
